points.text: Between pieces of text, + joins them. It adds no space — you add your own.

points.text: Left to right. "1"+2 is already text, so 3 gets glued on: 123.

points.label: no counter

lessons.title: Arithmetic Expressions
objectives: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
predict the result of integer division
use the modulo operator to find remainders

points.text: Add, subtract, multiply. * is a star, not an ×.
Divide. It behaves differently for whole numbers than you expect — that's coming up.
Remainder. 7 % 2 is 1, because 2 goes into 7 three times with 1 left over.
Brackets, to force what happens first.

steps.instruction: Java does maths with these six symbols.

steps.after: Exactly like a calculator. The interesting part is next.
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
steps.instruction: Run it. Nothing surprising yet.

steps.code: System.out.println(2 + 3 * 4);

points.text: * and / and % happen BEFORE + and -. Same rule you already use in maths class.
points.label: first

points.text: 2 + 3 * 4 is 2 + 12, which is 14. It is NOT 5 * 4.
points.label: so

points.text: Put brackets around what you want to happen first.
points.label: override

steps.instruction: When there's more than one operator, order matters.

steps.why: Brackets go first, so it's 5 * 4 = 20. Without them it would have been 14.
steps.code: System.out.println((2 + 3) * 4);
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
steps.instruction: Brackets added. Now what?

steps.code: System.out.println(7 / 2);

points.text: When BOTH numbers are whole numbers, Java throws away the fraction. It does not round.
points.label: 3, not 3.5

points.text: A whole number divided by a whole number has to stay a whole number. 3.5 can't fit, so the .5 is dropped.
points.label: why

points.text: Gives 4, not 4.5 and not 5. Always chops downward.
Make one of them a decimal: 7.0 / 2 gives 3.5.
points.label: want 3.5?

steps.instruction: Now the one that catches everybody.

steps.why: Both are whole numbers, so the .5 is thrown away and you get 4.
steps.code: System.out.println(9 / 2);
skills: predict the result of integer division
steps.instruction: So what does this print?

steps.why: The division happens FIRST, as whole numbers, giving 4. Only then is 4 stored in a double. Storing it in a double afterwards can't bring the .5 back — it prints 4.0.
steps.code:
double avg = 9 / 2;
System.out.println(avg);
skills: predict the result of integer division
steps.instruction: This one looks safe but isn't. Tap the line that goes wrong.

skills: predict the result of integer division
steps.instruction: Make it print the real average, 4.5.

points.text: 2 fits into 7 three times (6), and 1 is left over. So 1.
5 fits exactly, nothing left over. So 0.
A remainder of 0 means it divides evenly — that's how you test if a number is even, or a multiple of anything.
points.label: 0 means

steps.instruction: % gives you what's left over.

steps.code:

System.out.println(20 % 4);

questions.why: 4 fits exactly 5 times, nothing left over.

steps.hint: One of them counts how many fit. The other is what refuses to fit.

lessons.title: Logical Operators
objectives: combine two booleans with && and ||
flip a boolean with !
work out the value of an expression that mixes them

steps.instruction: && means BOTH have to be true.

points.text: Two ampersands. Read it as "and".

points.label: both true
points.text: true && true is the only combination that gives true.

points.label: one false
points.text: If either side is false, the whole thing is false.

steps.instruction: Run it.
steps.after: && is strict. Everything must be true.

steps.instruction: What prints?
steps.code: System.out.println(false && true);
steps.why: && needs both sides true. The first is false, so the answer is false.
skills: combine two booleans with && and ||

steps.instruction: || means AT LEAST ONE has to be true.
steps.code:
System.out.println(true || false);
System.out.println(false || false);

points.text: Two pipe characters, above the backslash key. Read it as "or".

points.label: one is enough
points.text: true || false is true. Only one side needs to hold up.

points.label: both false
points.text: The only way to get false is if neither side is true.

steps.instruction: And this one?
steps.code: System.out.println(false || true);
steps.why: || only needs one side to be true, and the second one is.
skills: combine two booleans with && and ||

steps.instruction: ! flips a boolean to its opposite.

points.text: An exclamation mark in front. Read it as "not".

points.label: !true
points.text: Becomes false. !false becomes true. It just swaps.

points.label: true && !false
points.text: Do the ! first: !false is true. So it is true && true, which is true.

points.label: order
points.text: ! happens before && and ||, the same way × happens before +.

steps.instruction: Work these out.
steps.code:
boolean a = true;
boolean b = false;
skills: work out the value of an expression that mixes them

steps.instruction: Fill in the operator so it prints false.
steps.hint: Which one refuses when only ONE side is true?
steps.after: && is the strict one. || is the generous one.
skills: combine two booleans with && and ||

lessons.title: Comparison Operators
objectives: compare two values to get true or false

steps.instruction: Comparing two numbers gives you a boolean.

points.label: > and <
points.text: Greater than, less than. Exactly like maths class.

points.label: >= and <=
points.text: Greater-or-equal, less-or-equal. 80 >= 80 is true, because equal counts.

points.label: the result
points.text: A comparison is not a number. It comes back as true or false — a boolean.

steps.instruction: Run it.
steps.after: Every comparison answers one yes/no question.

steps.instruction: What prints?
steps.code: System.out.println(5 <= 4);
steps.why: 5 is not less than 4, and it is not equal to 4 either. So false.
skills: choose between ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=

steps.instruction: == asks a question. = gives an answer.

points.text: TWO equals signs. Asks "are these the same?" and gives back true or false.
ONE equals sign. Puts a value into a box. It does not ask anything.
Not equal. The ! means "not", the same as last lesson.

points.label: the classic bug
points.text: Writing = when you meant == is the single most common mistake in this unit.

steps.instruction: A score of exactly 7 should count as a pass, but this says false. Tap the line at fault.
steps.why: > means strictly greater, so 7 does not count. It should be >= to include 7 itself.

lessons.title: For Loops
objectives: trace a for-loop's counter through each iteration
predict how many times a loop body runs
write a for-loop that counts to a target

points.text: Where the counter starts. It runs once, at the very beginning.
points.label: int i = 1

points.text: Checked before every turn. While it is true the block runs; the moment it is false the loop stops.
points.label: i <= 5

points.text: Runs after each turn. It adds 1 to i — without it the loop would never end.
points.label: i++

points.text: Everything inside { } is what gets repeated.
points.label: the braces

steps.instruction: A for loop repeats a block a set number of times.

steps.after: One line of code, five lines of output. That's a loop.
skills: write a for-loop that counts to a target
steps.instruction: This repeats itself. Run it.

steps.hint: Only one number decides where it stops.
steps.after: The middle part is the stop condition — it decides when to quit.
skills: write a for-loop that counts to a target
steps.instruction: Make it count to 10 instead.

points.text: Three turns — but the numbers stop at 2, because < 3 is false when i reaches 3.
Start at 0 with <, or start at 1 with <=. Both give you N turns. Mixing them up is the classic off-by-one.
points.label: < vs <=

points.text: You will see this everywhere in Java, so it is worth getting used to now.
points.label: why 0

steps.instruction: Counting from 0 is the normal way to repeat N times.

steps.why: i < 5 stops BEFORE 5, so it runs on 1,2,3,4 — four times, not five. This one character is the most common loop bug there is.
skills: predict how many times a loop body runs
steps.instruction: Note the < instead of <=. What prints?

steps.why: Starting at 0 and stopping before 3 gives 0,1,2 — three runs. Starting at 0 with < is the standard way to repeat something N times.
skills: predict how many times a loop body runs
steps.instruction: How many x's?

skills: trace a for-loop's counter through each iteration

questions.why: i starts at 1, so i * 10 is 10.

questions.prompt: and the last thing it prints?

questions.why: i takes the values 1, 2, 3 — three passes, three lines.

steps.instruction: Follow i.

steps.why: That line drags i back to 1 on every pass, so i++ can never get it past 3. The body can change the counter — and that's how loops get stuck.
skills: trace a for-loop's counter through each iteration
steps.instruction: Tap the line that makes this run forever.

points.text: The last part is just "what to do after each turn". It can be anything.
points.label: i = i + 2

points.text: The short way of writing the same thing.
points.label: i += 2

points.text: Counts DOWN. Start high and end low for a countdown.
points.label: i--

steps.instruction: The counter does not have to go up by one.

steps.hint: Start on the first even number, and step by how far apart evens are.
steps.after: The third part doesn't have to be i++ — you can step by any amount.
skills: write a for-loop that counts to a target

lessons.title: If Statements
objectives: run a block of code only when a condition is true
use else to handle the other case
use the remainder operator inside a condition

steps.instruction: An if statement runs a block only when something is true.

points.label: if (…)
points.text: The condition goes in round brackets. It has to be something true-or-false — exactly what you built last lesson.

points.label: the braces
points.text: Everything inside { } runs only when the condition is true.

points.label: "done"
points.text: Outside the braces, so it prints either way. Indentation is for you; the braces are what Java reads.

points.label: no semicolon
points.text: There is no ; after the round brackets. Putting one there is a classic bug.

steps.instruction: Run it.
steps.after: The condition was true, so the block ran.

steps.instruction: Change the age so "adult" does NOT print.
steps.hint: The condition is age >= 18. Make it false.
steps.after: False condition, block skipped — and the line after it still runs.
skills: run a block of code only when a condition is true

steps.instruction: else covers the other case.

points.label: else
points.text: Runs when the condition was false. No condition of its own.

points.label: one or the other
points.text: Exactly one of the two blocks runs. Never both, never neither.

points.label: } else {
points.text: else sits on the closing brace of the if.

steps.instruction: n is 0 this time. What prints?
steps.why: 0 is not greater than 0, so the condition is false and else runs. Zero catches people out constantly.
skills: use else to handle the other case

steps.instruction: The remainder tells you if a number is even.

points.label: n % 2
points.text: The remainder after dividing by 2 — from the arithmetic lesson. It is 0 or 1.
Asks whether that remainder is zero. Remainder 0 means it divided evenly.

points.label: together
points.text: n % 2 == 0 is THE way to test for even. Worth memorising.
7 % 2 is 1, not 0, so the condition is false and else runs.

steps.instruction: 8 is even, but this says odd. Fix it.
steps.hint: What remainder does an even number leave when you divide by 2?
steps.after: Remainder 0 is even, remainder 1 is odd. The condition was testing the wrong one.
skills: use the remainder operator inside a condition

steps.instruction: else if lets you check several things in order.

points.label: top to bottom
points.text: Java checks each condition in order and stops at the first true one.

points.label: the rest are skipped
points.text: Once one matches, none of the others are even looked at.

points.label: else last
points.text: The final else catches everything that matched nothing.
Not >= 90, not >= 80, so it falls through to else.

steps.instruction: Fill it in so min ends up holding the smaller number.
steps.hint: Replace min only when b is SMALLER than what is already there.
steps.after: Assume the first is smallest, then replace it if you find better. That scales to any number of values.
skills: run a block of code only when a condition is true

lessons.title: Loop-and-a-Half
objectives: use break to leave a loop from the middle
write a while (true) loop that asks once and checks once
stop a loop on a sentinel value

steps.instruction: Here is the problem this lesson solves.
steps.output:
Enter your guess: 4
Try again!
Enter your guess: 6
Correct!

points.label: it works
points.text: The output is right. Nothing here is broken.

points.label: but look
points.text: The readInt line appears TWICE — once before the loop, once inside it.

points.label: why
points.text: A while loop checks its condition first, so you must already have a guess before the loop can start.

points.label: the risk
points.text: Two copies of the same line means two places to change, and one you will forget.

steps.instruction: Run it. We'll guess 4, then 6.
steps.after: Correct output, duplicated line. Now the better way.

steps.instruction: Loop forever, and break out of the middle.
steps.output:
Enter your guess: 4
Try again!
Enter your guess: 6
Correct!

points.label: while (true)
points.text: A condition that is always true, so the loop never stops on its own.

points.label: break;
points.text: Jumps straight out of the loop, immediately, ignoring everything below it.

points.label: asked once
points.text: readInt now appears exactly once. That is the whole point.

points.label: the "half"
points.text: On the last pass only the top half runs — you ask, you check, you leave before "Try again!".

steps.instruction: Same answers, same output — one copy of the question.
steps.after: This shape has a name: the loop-and-a-half.
skills: write a while (true) loop that asks once and checks once

steps.instruction: break works in any loop. What prints?
steps.why: When i reaches 3 the break runs before the println, and the loop ends entirely — it does not skip one and carry on.
skills: use break to leave a loop from the middle

steps.instruction: Tap the only line that can end this loop.
steps.why: while (true) is never false, so nothing else can stop it. Take the break away and it runs forever.
skills: use break to leave a loop from the middle

steps.instruction: A sentinel is a value that means "stop".
steps.output:
Number (0 to stop): 5
Number (0 to stop): 7
Number (0 to stop): 0
12

points.label: sentinel
points.text: Here it is 0 — a value the user types to say they are finished.

points.label: say so
points.text: The prompt tells them what it is. A secret sentinel is a broken program.

points.label: not counted
points.text: The break happens before the adding, so the 0 never joins the total. 5 + 7 = 12.

points.label: choosing one
points.text: Pick something that cannot be real data — 0 marks here, -1 for a temperature.

steps.instruction: Fill in the statement that leaves the loop.
steps.target:
Number (0 to stop): 5
5
Number (0 to stop): 0
steps.hint: You want out of the loop entirely, not on to the next turn.
steps.after: break leaves the loop. That is the one statement this whole lesson rests on.
skills: use break to leave a loop from the middle
